::: {.chapter-subtitle}
A claim to test, not a creed to defend.

## The view from the other shore

Imagine the world economy not from London or New York but from a beach on the Malabar
coast, or the deck of a dhow running before the monsoon from Aden to Gujarat. It is a
deliberately awkward place to stand, because almost every long-run history of the world
economy is written from somewhere else — from the North Atlantic, looking outward, with
Europe as the active party and the rest of the world as the stage on which European energy
plays out. Tell the story that way and its shape is settled in advance: the world is poor and
static until, around 1500 or 1750, Europe stirs, and modern prosperity radiates from a single
source.

Stand on the Indian Ocean shore instead and a different shape appears. You notice that for
most of recorded history the largest and richest economies, and the most commercially
developed, were in Asia — Han and Song China, the Abbasid caliphate, Mughal India — and that
the world's most coveted store of value, silver and gold, flowed toward them, not away.
Europe, by contrast, spent long centuries as a periphery: an exporter of slaves, furs and raw
metal, an importer of manufactures and ideas, paying for what it wanted in bullion it could
barely produce itself. And the period in which Europe genuinely ran the world economy is
short — concentrated in the century or so after 1750 — and even at its height it rested on the
Asian periphery it governed.

This book takes that view seriously enough to build a whole history around it. But the vantage
point is a tool, not a slogan. The argument it generates is a claim, and the book's job is to
test that claim, period by period, against what the evidence will bear, and to be candid about
where the evidence is thin and where serious scholars disagree.

The complaint about where world history starts is not this book's invention, and it is worth
seeing how the field states it. David Northrup observes that textbooks "almost invariably" break
their coverage at 1500, and Merry Wiesner-Hanks, introducing the *Cambridge World History*, names
the problem in her own preface while conceding that four of that series' nine books are given to
1400 and after. Northrup pushes the point further back than 1500, and in a form that reaches this
book's own starting line: the deeper exclusion is the convention of beginning with Sumer and with
writing, which removes something between 95 and 99.6 per cent of the human past from the story
before it starts.

There are honest defences of the imbalance, and readers should have them. David Christian argues
the demographic case: perhaps eighty per cent of all human lives were lived between the Palaeolithic
and 1750, which is an argument for weighting the deep past, but the counter-argument is that
evidence, not lives, is what a historian can work with, and evidence accumulates toward the present.
Wiesner-Hanks makes exactly that case for the series' shape. And one chapter in the same volume goes
after this book's method rather than its coverage: Michael Lang argues that periodising by
chronology, which is precisely what the ten-chapter structure ahead does, smuggles in assumptions
about what changes and when. That objection is not answered here. It is worth carrying while
reading.

One thing the methodological literature does not supply is a way to put numbers on the deep past.
There is no toolkit for reconstructing prices before there are prices. Chapters 1 and 2 have to work
without them, and say so.^[**Sources:** Northrup, "Globalization in historical perspective", in *The
Cambridge World History*, vol. 1 (2015), pp. 110-31, at pp. 111-12 and 123; Wiesner-Hanks, preface
to vol. 1, pp. xvii and xix; Christian, "Introduction: the constructions of a global past", vol. 1,
pp. 22-23, on the demographic weighting; Lang, "Evolution, rupture, and periodization", vol. 1,
pp. 84-109, at pp. 96-97, on chronology-first periodisation. **Read more:** Sachsenmaier, "The
evolution of world histories", vol. 1, pp. 56-83.]

## The spine: the claim we are testing

Here is the argument in one paragraph; the rest of the book interrogates it.

> *Viewed from the Indian Ocean, the world economy spent most of its history centred on
> Asia — visible in the direction bullion flowed and in where the world's goods were made.
> Integration advanced and retreated in waves shaped by climate, disease, technology and
> money, along a durable maritime channel and a periodically resurgent overland one. Europe's
> dominance was real and transformative but bounded — concentrated in the century after
> 1750, built partly on the Asian centrality it overturned, and resting at its height on the
> Indian Ocean periphery it governed. Its timing and depth remain debated, and the East's
> aggregate return — measurable but partial, achieved within a Western-built order — is the
> long arc closing, not simply repeating.*

Call this the spine. It treats European dominance as an interruption rather than a
destination, but a bounded one. Four qualifications bound the claim, and they recur throughout
the book:

1. the interruption was consequential — roughly two transformative centuries, not a blip;
2. its timing and depth are genuinely open, debated in @sec-ch07 over the Great Divergence;
3. the eventual return east is partial — aggregate weight, not a restoration of per-capita
   parity; and
4. it is system-dependent — the Asian re-rise happened within a US-anchored order.

We do not settle the spine here. We assemble the tools to test it, and return to weigh it in
the [Conclusion](11-conclusion.qmd).

## What "centre of gravity" measures

The spine is a claim about where the weight of the world economy sat. A claim like that is only
as good as its definition of weight, so here is the one this book uses.

**Weight is output.** The centre of gravity is the point world economic activity balances around,
and the quantity being balanced is production. Not territory, not population for its own sake, and
not the volume of trade for its own sake.

**Before about 1800, output is read through population.** In a Malthusian world more food meant
more people rather than richer people, so income per head moved within a narrow band and a region's
share of world output tracked its share of world population closely. That is a convenience and a
limitation at once, and the circularity deserves stating plainly: most historical output estimates
for the pre-modern world were themselves built from population figures and assumed income levels,
so the agreement between the two series before 1800 is partly a fact about the world and partly an
artefact of how the numbers were made. Where a chapter rests on population, it says so.

**Not all output counts equally.** What the spine is about is the *connected* economy: output that
trade enabled, or that was produced for trade, and above all for long-distance trade. A subsistence
farmer's grain is output, and in aggregate it dwarfs everything else in every chapter before the
nineteenth century — but it never moved, and it cannot move a centre of gravity. So the weighting
favours the goods that travelled, the workshops that made them and the ports that handled them.
This is why a chapter can call Rome the largest single economy of its age and still place the centre
of gravity east of it. The two statements measure different things and both are true.

**Bullion indicates; it does not define.** The direction metal flowed is this book's running tracer,
because metal moved toward the workshop. It is evidence for where the centre lay, and good evidence,
but it is not what the centre *is*.

**Two instruments, not one.** For nine chapters the centre has to be inferred — from city sizes,
trade composition, the direction of bullion, shares of world manufacturing. In @sec-ch10 it can also
be computed: Danny Quah's economic centre of gravity, the distance-weighted average location of
world output. That calculation is offered there as a **complement** to the reading this book has
been making all along, not as a replacement for it. It weights all output equally, so it answers a
slightly different question from the one asked in the preceding chapters, and the two readings are
worth holding side by side rather than collapsing into one.

**One switch, announced in advance.** Chapters 1 to 6 score aggregate weight; from @sec-ch07 the
measure that matters becomes income per head. That switch is not a lapse — it *is* the Great
Divergence, and the chapter says so — but it does mean the early and late verdicts are not marks on
the same ruler.

**Confidence.** Every verdict carries a level, and the levels mean this. *Low* — the direction is a
reasonable reading of the evidence, and a different reading would not be unreasonable. *Moderate* —
the direction is supported by more than one independent kind of evidence, while the magnitude is
contested. *High* — several independent measures point the same way and the disagreement in the
literature is about explanation rather than direction. Confidence rises across the book because the
evidence improves, not because the argument gets better.

## The four questions

The book asks the same four questions of every period. They organise every chapter and are the
method the book hands you. Together they answer the spine — *where is the centre of gravity,
and is it moving?* — without pre-judging it.

::: {.callout-important}
## The four motivating questions
- **Q1 — Direction.** Is the system integrating or disintegrating? (Two refinements the
  evidence forces on the simple cycle: integration breeds fragility, since the links that carry
  goods carry shocks; and disintegration has winners, since a fracturing core can loosen its
  grip on a periphery.)
- **Q2 — Channels.** Which routes carry the integrating weight, maritime or overland, and are
  they complements or substitutes? (The maritime Indian Ocean is the durable artery; the
  overland corridor had one true climax, the Mongol Pax of @sec-ch04.)
- **Q3 — Modes.** Which of the four flows — goods, technology, people, capital — is doing the
  integrating? Here the book makes one move: treat bullion as a *good* until the nineteenth
  century, then as *money and capital* after, and read its direction as the running tracer of
  the centre of gravity.
- **Q4 — Europe.** What is Europe's role — peripheral, entrant, dominant, one of several
  cores — and how does it change? Asked as an open question, not assumed.
:::

The spine is answered jointly by Q3, which follows the bullion and then the capital, and Q4,
Europe's changing role; Q1 and Q2 describe how the system that holds the centre is wired at
each moment. The arc the four questions trace, chapter by chapter, is this:

> no single centre (Ch 1) $\to$ Asia the production-centre of a multipolar relay (Ch 2) $\to$
> Asia central, Europe peripheral (Ch 3) $\to$ Asia central, a first north-west-European seed
> (Ch 4) $\to$ Asia the silver sink (Ch 5) $\to$ Asia the workshop, Europe armed (Ch 6) $\to$
> the turning point, the centre moves west (Ch 7) $\to$ peak Western dominance on an Indian-Ocean
> base (Ch 8) $\to$ the order cracks within the West (Ch 9) $\to$ the return toward Asia (Ch 10).

### The bullion tracer, and why it flips

Before modern capital markets, metal moved toward the workshop. People who made things the
rest of the world wanted — Indian cotton, Chinese silk and porcelain — were paid in silver and
gold, which pooled where production was most valued. So in antiquity Roman silver drained
*east* to India (@sec-ch02); in the early-modern centuries New World silver flowed *east* to
China (@sec-ch05). The tracer even works in reverse where it should: the Abbasid core paid
silver *north* to its slave-and-fur periphery (@sec-ch03), mirroring Rome.

After the nineteenth century the logic flips, because bullion's role changes. Under the
classical gold standard and integrated capital markets, gold becomes money and capital, and
following it leads not to the workshop but to the financial core — London, then New York. But
note who underwrote that core: India's colonial "drain" helped finance Britain's payments
deficits (@sec-ch08), sourced in the periphery and intermediated by the core.

## Six threads that run the length of the book

Beyond the four questions, six threads run through the book; this section sets them out.

1. **Centre of gravity** — the spine itself, tracked with an explicit verdict entered for each
   period and a stated confidence level in every chapter.
2. **Measurement of success: quantity to quality.** This thread corrects a recurring error.
   Before about 1800, like every other species, humans turned prosperity into numbers — more
   people, more output, bigger empires (aggregate, *extensive* growth). Only after about 1800
   did any society turn it into sustained income per head (per-capita, *intensive* growth, the
   escape from the Malthusian ceiling, and a uniquely modern one). The thread is set up in
   @sec-ch01, runs through the silver story in @sec-ch05 and @sec-ch06, and resolves at
   @sec-ch07, where the Great Divergence *is* the switch. It is what stops us reading every
   "thriving" empire — Han, Song, Mughal, Qing — as growth in the modern sense.
3. **Follow the silver** — the early-modern form of the bullion tracer (@sec-ch05 to
   @sec-ch07). The same American silver met different monetary conditions and so had different
   fates: Asia absorbed and specialised, the Ottomans inflated, West Africa debased and
   depleted, and Europe converted its monetary loss into armed-trade and financial power. That
   last fate is the bridge to the divergence.
4. **Measurement of integration: how we know.** The evidence for measuring integration improves
   over time, from the diffusion of goods and ideas, to bullion flows, to wages and prices, to
   GDP, to a computed centre of gravity. Before prices, only the diffusion prong exists, which
   limits what @sec-ch01 and @sec-ch02 can claim.
5. **Forces.** Four drivers sit behind Q1's direction — climate, disease, technology, policy —
   two of them natural, a reminder that the world economy has always been embedded in a natural
   system.
6. **Data survival and bias.** What survives reflects record-keeping conventions and the
   accidents of climate and preservation. Absence of data is not absence of activity, and the
   surviving record under-documents the very Indian-Ocean world this book centres on. Whose
   eyes we see through is itself a running question.

## A note on method

Two commitments follow, and they are why the subtitle is *data and debates*.

Before those, three pieces of measurement apparatus that the chapters use rather than re-derive.

**How integration is measured.** From the eighth chapter onward it is read off price convergence,
and the test is not that the same good costs the same in two places — it never does. The test is that
the gap between the two prices is bounded by the cost of moving the good, and narrows as that cost
falls. A stable price gap between two trading places is therefore not a market failing to integrate;
it is the cost of integration, quoted. Before quoted prices exist the test cannot be run, and
integration has to be read a cruder way: from the diffusion of goods and the spread of shared
standards, which establishes that two economies touched and says almost nothing about how much, how
often, or at what price.

**The two yardsticks.** The book measures two different things and keeps them apart. *Integration* is
the question above. *Success* is a separate one, and before about 1800 it means aggregate weight —
more people, more output, bigger cities — not income per head. The switch to per-capita measurement
happens at the Great Divergence of @sec-ch07, and it is announced there because it *is* the
Divergence.

**Absence of data is not absence of activity.** What survives reflects record-keeping conventions and
the accidents of preservation, not economic weight. Organic records rot in the humid monsoon tropics
and survive in cool, dry Europe and arid Egypt, so the surviving record systematically
under-documents the ocean world this book centres on. Survival can be perverse: Mesopotamia's tablets
were unbaked clay, and what fired them hard was the burning of the palaces that held them, so the
densest evidence for the Bronze Age economy is a by-product of catastrophe. The rule cuts in one
direction only. A known one-way bias makes the surviving record a *lower bound* on activity in the
under-documented places, which licenses claims about direction and licenses nothing about magnitude —
and it is not a warrant for treating thin evidence as evidence for the argument.

- **Data.** The book leans on numbers — trade volumes, bullion flows, real wages, output
  shares, the computed centre of gravity — because numbers are how you adjudicate a claim like
  the spine rather than just asserting it. The figures and tables are reproducible: generated
  from datasets you can download and re-run. But the data thin out sharply as you go back, and
  they are biased toward the literate, fiscal, European end of the record. A chapter on the
  Bronze Age and a chapter on the twentieth century are not equally evidenced, and the book
  says so.
- **Debates.** Where the scholarship is genuinely contested — when the Great Divergence began
  and why; whether interwar disintegration was man-made or inevitable; when "globalisation"
  really started — the book presents the disagreement rather than resolving it out of sight.
  Disputed figures are flagged and taught, not silently resolved. The aim is to hand you the
  questions, the evidence and the open arguments, so you can test the spine yourself.

::: {.callout-note}
## How to read the chapters
Each chapter opens by following one object that carries its period's story, locates the period
on the arc, sets out the cast and how we know, narrates the period on its own terms, then reads
it through the four questions, delivers a centre-of-gravity verdict with a confidence level,
and hands off to the next. Look out for the recurring Data exhibit and Debate, and the Follow
the money and How we know callouts.
:::
